title: Dyer v. National By-Products, Inc.
summary: An invalid claim can still support a settlement through good-faith forbearance. Whether Dyer honestly held the claim remained a factual question, so summary judgment was premature.

sections.Parties: Dale Dyer sued his employer, National By-Products, alleging breach of an oral lifetime-employment promise made in exchange for giving up a personal-injury claim.
sections.Material Facts:
Dyer lost his right foot in a workplace accident. The employer placed him on paid leave, then he returned as a foreman and was later laid off indefinitely. Dyer alleged that he had refrained from suing because the employer promised lifetime employment. The employer denied making that promise.

For purposes of the appeal, the court assumed that the proposed tort claim was invalid because workers’ compensation supplied the relevant remedy. It did not assume that Dyer knew the claim was invalid. The distinction between the claim’s legal weakness and Dyer’s honest understanding was the central issue.
sections.Procedural History: The district court granted summary judgment for the employer, reasoning that Dyer had given no reciprocal lifetime-work promise and had surrendered no viable claim. The Supreme Court of Iowa reversed and remanded because a material factual question about good faith remained. It did not find that the lifetime promise had actually been made or that Dyer had proved every element of recovery.
sections.Issue: Does surrender of a legally invalid claim necessarily fail as consideration, or can an honest belief in the claim support enforcement of the alleged settlement?
sections.Holding: Invalidity alone did not establish lack of consideration as a matter of law. The court adopted the approach reflected in Restatement § 74 and required examination of Dyer’s good faith.
sections.Reasoning:
Settlement enables parties to avoid the expense and uncertainty of resolving disputed claims. Reopening every settlement whenever the underlying claim turns out to fail would undermine that function. The court preferred an approach allowing good-faith compromise even where the claim ultimately lacks legal foundation, and overruled inconsistent Iowa holdings.

Good faith was not satisfied merely by saying “I believed it.” The objective weakness of the claim could be evidence that the asserted belief was not honestly held. The opinion therefore distinguishes the legal validity of the underlying tort claim from the factual sincerity of the claimant. Other jurisdictions described in the opinion imposed more demanding objective limits; the Iowa court’s choice should remain attributed to it. On remand, the promise and the good-faith surrender still required proof.

priorVersions.summary: Forbearance of an invalid claim may be consideration when the claimant honestly and fairly believes it valid; the remand left that factual inquiry open.
priorVersions.notes:
Court: Supreme Court of Iowa (1986).

The notes compare Fiege v. Boehm’s paternity settlement, good faith, pleading obligations, and other waivers. Treat those comparisons as boundary questions, not a license to assert a claim known to be false.

sections.Parties: Dyer, an employee who lost a foot in an accident, sued National By-Products, his employer.
sections.Material Facts: Dyer alleged that the employer promised lifetime employment in exchange for his forbearance of a personal-injury claim. The employer disputed the alleged agreement. The claim he said he surrendered was legally invalid under the applicable compensation regime. He was later laid off.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court granted summary judgment for the employer on the ground that the invalid claim could not supply consideration. The Supreme Court of Iowa reversed and remanded. It did not establish that the alleged promise, bargain, or good-faith belief had been proved.
sections.Issue: Can forbearance of a claim lacking legal merit support a settlement bargain when the claimant believes the claim is valid?
sections.Holding: An honest, good-faith belief may make forbearance sufficient despite the claim’s legal invalidity. The claimant’s good faith required further consideration rather than categorical rejection solely for lack of a valid underlying claim.
sections.Reasoning: The policy supporting compromise would be undermined if every settlement depended on later proof that the surrendered claim would have won. The opinion uses Restatement § 74’s distinction between a doubtful claim and a claim believed fairly capable of being determined valid. Objective weakness may bear on whether a professed belief is honest. A knowingly baseless or bad-faith nuisance claim is not insulated by merely calling its abandonment consideration.

learning.why: Dyer shows why a statement of the rule needs the procedural posture attached. The appeal preserved a possible claim; it did not conclusively establish a binding lifetime-employment agreement.

topics.consideration: The claimed exchange was forbearance for job security.
topics.forbearance: The legal invalidity of the surrendered claim is not automatically decisive.
topics.good-faith: Here good faith concerns an honest assertion of a claim, not performance of an existing contract.
topics.proof: Summary judgment could not resolve the remaining factual issue.
